content: Ammonium chloride (NH4Cl), also known by various names such as sal ammoniac, salmiac, nushadir salt, and others, is a clear, white, water-soluble crystalline salt derived from ammonia in its pure form. When dissolved in water, ammonium chloride forms a mildly acidic solution. The term ammonium originates from sal ammoniac, a name historically used for this compound. In Arabic-speaking countries and Persia, it was referred to as nushadir salt, while in China it was called naosha, and in India, nao sadar. The Romans named the ammonium chloride deposits they collected near the Temple of Jupiter Ammon in ancient Libya sal ammoniacus (salt of Ammon) due to their proximity to the temple. This compound was considered one of the four alchemical spirits. Its dissociation into ammonia and hydrochloric acid, both corrosive substances capable of attacking metals, led some alchemists to believe it might hold the secret to transmuting metals. However, in Arabic traditions, it was primarily used as a source of ammonia. In nature, ammonium chloride is found in volcanic regions, forming on volcanic rocks near vents that release fumes. The crystals deposit directly from the gaseous state but are short-lived as they dissolve easily in water. Commercially, ammonium chloride is synthesized by reacting ammonia (NH3) with hydrogen chloride (HCl). Ammonium chloride has a variety of applications. It is sold in blocks at hardware stores for cleaning the tips of soldering irons and is sometimes included in solder as a flux. It is also used as a feed supplement for cattle, in hair shampoos, in textile printing, in the adhesive for bonding plywood, as an ingredient in nutritive media for yeast, in cleaning products, and as a component in cough medicine. Its expectorant action is due to its irritative effect on the bronchial mucosa, which stimulates the production of excess respiratory tract fluid, making it easier to expel through coughing. Additionally, it is employed in oral acid-loading tests to diagnose distal renal tubular acidosis. Ammonium chloride is used in snow treatment, particularly on ski slopes at temperatures above 0°C, to harden the snow and slow its melting. In several countries, it is added to licorice-type dark candies (e.g., Finland's salmiakki, Sweden's lakrisal, the Netherlands' zoute drop, and Denmark's Dracula Piller) and as a flavoring for vodkas. Medically, ammonium chloride serves as an expectorant, diuretic, and systemic acidifying agent. It is used in the treatment of severe metabolic alkalosis, to maintain an acidic urine pH in certain urinary tract disorders, or in forced acid diuresis. However, ammonium salts can irritate the gastric mucosa, potentially causing nausea and vomiting.
